j.learned_fact: A person measures a little taller in the morning than at night (true: spinal discs compress over the day), shown through repeated wall measurements.
j.thinking_skill: Inferring a pattern (morning tall, night small) from three repeated measurements
j.notes: 'It was snowy outside, so the roof was warm and loud' is a non-sequitur; the story never hints at why height changes, so a 4-year-old may take it as magic rather than a real body fact.

j.learned_fact: Yeast is a living thing that eats sugar and gives off gas bubbles, which is what makes dough rise (true).
j.thinking_skill: Revising a misconception ('the dough is alive') after the teacher's correction
j.notes: The premise is forced: a music teacher makes real dough so a child can sing about bread, and the yeast fact is delivered as an explicit teacher definition rather than discovered.

j.learned_fact: Vatican City is the smallest country (walkable in about twenty minutes) and Russia stretches across eleven time zones; both true.
j.thinking_skill: Following a four-step sequence (first/next/then/last) and estimating that the task will take more than one day
j.notes: The sequence words are bolted on ('First the globe, next the stickers, then the map, last the hug'), and 195 countries and eleven time zones are abstract for a 5-year-old; counting to 195 on fingers is silly rather than childlike.

j.learned_fact: Pacing with feet gives different answers for different people because feet differ in size; a ruler gives everyone the same answer (the need for a standard unit).
j.thinking_skill: Explaining a measurement discrepancy by identifying the changing variable (foot size) and valuing a shared standard tool
j.notes: The teacher 'sprinkled some paper stars on the rug' is a random detail with no purpose, and 'forty marks' never names a unit, missing the easy chance to introduce inches or centimetres.

j.learned_fact: Velcro was invented by Swiss engineer George de Mestral after he studied burrs stuck in his dog's fur; burrs cling by tiny hooks catching loops (true).
j.thinking_skill: Analogical transfer: examining how a burr's hooks grip loops and applying the mechanism to a new design
j.notes: The dad's Velcro trivia arrives as a convenient coincidence at the end, and sewing a strip of actual burrs onto felt as a working fastener is a stretch.

j.learned_fact: Old Venice has no cars: mail, groceries and even ambulances travel by boat, and the city is more than a hundred islands joined by bridges (true).
j.thinking_skill: Sorting by two attributes at once (size and weight) after discovering that bigger does not mean heavier
j.notes: 'Daring' is misused (a boat ambulance is not daring) and the 'fancy mammal in a feather coat' joke risks teaching a 9-year-old that birds are mammals; the mask-sorting thread and the Venice thread never connect, and the mail parade, bell and accordion are decorative filler.

j.learned_fact: Sound travels about four times faster through water and about fifteen times faster through steel than through air, which is why an ear on a rail hears a train before the sound arrives through the air (true).
j.thinking_skill: Repeating a trial to rule out imagination, then applying a remembered principle to explain the observation and transfer it to keeping time
j.notes: Grammar error 'Dylan persevere anyway'; the door-swollen-shut set-up is contrived, and over a hallway the two arrivals would be tens of milliseconds apart, so hearing a clear double beat is exaggerated.

j.learned_fact: Tapping a bottle makes the glass-plus-water ring, so a fuller bottle sounds lower; blowing across it makes the air inside vibrate, so a fuller bottle (less air) sounds higher (true).
j.thinking_skill: Inferring that two different vibrating media explain opposite pitch orderings, tested by systematic back-to-back comparison
j.notes: 'The revolution came at dinner' misuses 'revolution', 'I hypothesize' is forced banter, and there is a pronoun slip ('lied to her on purpose' should be 'him'); reads a shade young for 13.

j.learned_fact: Water's boiling point depends on pressure: at about twice atmospheric pressure (a pressure cooker) it boils near 120 C and food cooks faster; at high altitude it boils below 100 C and food takes longer (true).
j.thinking_skill: Changing one variable (sealed lid) and inferring that the hidden variable is water temperature, not boiling itself
j.notes: No reason is ever given why rice would stay hard after forty minutes in an open pot on an ordinary stove, so the premise is unmotivated; the brass pendulum clock is padding and the closing line ('borrowed her pendulum clock's patience') is nonsense.

j.learned_fact: A site that can email you your old password is storing it in plaintext; good sites store an irreversible hash and force a reset instead (true). FALSE: turning 120 degrees four times does not draw a hexagon (it retraces a triangle), and turning 90 degrees three times draws three sides, not a 'clean square'.
j.thinking_skill: Changing one variable at a time when debugging, then reasoning from a symptom (plaintext email) to the underlying design flaw
j.notes: The turtle geometry is wrong twice, and Hunter's 'one thing at a time' rule is immediately broken when he changes angle and count together; 'feeling cordial about the whole afternoon' is a forced misuse, and the hashing explanation is a delivered mini-lecture.

j.learned_fact: Without any greenhouse effect Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 C instead of roughly 15 C; the effect is natural and the issue is how much stronger it has become (true).
j.thinking_skill: Conceding the opponent's valid point to reframe the debate, then recognizing that an average can hide distribution and causes
j.notes: Declan is a straw man ('effects aren't real things'), so the win is unearned; the story places the debate in a Grade 10 science class though the target is grade 11, and the sleet timeline (Thursday walk, Friday debate, 'walk home through the sleet' recalled before the vote) is muddled.

j.learned_fact: Coin flips have no memory: after five heads the next flip is still 50/50, yet a run of five or more shows up in nearly every hundred flips, so streaks are ordinary, not evidence that a result is 'due' (true; gambler's fallacy).
j.thinking_skill: Designing a simulation to discriminate two hypotheses, then checking the base rate of the observed event
j.notes: 'It couldn't implicate the coin of anything' misuses 'implicate'; the seeded random-number sub-plot is never explained to the reader (why deleting the seed number produces varying runs), so the first half is a mystery that just evaporates.

j.learned_fact: Recommendation feeds optimize for watch time rather than truth or usefulness, so whatever you watch longest you get more of; and evidence drawn only from the feed is circular, so you need an independent measure (true in broad terms).
j.thinking_skill: Recognizing that his evidence is circular and designing an independent baseline measure (mood before opening the app)
j.notes: The bug that squares 'his own name' into forty-nine is muddled and never makes sense; 'tautological' is stretched to mean 'circular' and 'eviscerate your whole evening' is showy, though 'epistemology' is used correctly and explained.

j.learned_fact: The first web page went online in 1991 at CERN, and Tim Berners-Lee persuaded CERN to release the web technology royalty-free in 1993 (true). FALSE detail: 4/5 read as month/day is April fifth, not 'April fourth' as the grandfather says.
j.thinking_skill: Holding two competing models (build-and-charge vs build-and-release) without forcing resolution, and distinguishing syntax errors from a semantically wrong but valid program
j.notes: The date-format twist gets its own arithmetic wrong (4/5 month-first is April 5, not April 4); 'foreboding and excitement at once' misuses 'foreboding' and 'equivocal' is a stretch for 'ambivalent'.
